prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence, from local labour-market designs, on how exposure to import competition and technological change shapes employment, wages and regional adjustment.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B020 and ranked B036 seventh. I now prefer B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, for three reasons that concern the substance of the work and not the number of colleagues who support it. First, my main objection was maturity: I worried that the unresolved debate on shift-share exposure measures, persistence and the role of automation meant the discovery was not yet settled. After reading the exchange, I think I conflated two things. The debate concerns long-run magnitudes. The central finding is that import exposure produced large, regionally concentrated and persistent local adjustment costs, and that finding has been replicated and has survived hostile re-examination in qualified form. That is what a prize should recognise. A contested size estimate does not undermine it. Second, the attribution is the most defensible on the shortlist. The seven round-1 supporters converge on one trio, and the core papers are jointly authored by those three. Third, the answers to the chair's question about my own B020 exposed a cost I had under-weighted. To reach a clean citation I had to narrow it to demand estimation. That leaves out Pakes' dynamic-oligopoly work and cuts across the claims of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. B036 has no comparable credit problem for the trade-shock core. The citation should rest on the design and the robust finding of persistent local adjustment, and it should not state an effect size. It should also not claim to credit the task-based theory of technology.
statement.case_against: The reservations I hold are the same ones I raised in round 1, now weighed differently. The ballot entry bundles the task and skill-bias strand with the trade-shock evidence, and a trio centred on the China shock leaves Katz and the task lineage uncredited. Acemoglu, recognised in 2024, and Levy and Murnane are outside the credited names. Magnitudes, long-run persistence, shift-share identification and the split between trade and automation are all still debated, so the citation must be worded cautiously. There is also thematic proximity to the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. As for B020, I still think random-coefficients demand estimation has the strongest combination of methodological reach and policy use of any candidate. I accept that it is a methods contribution rather than a discovery about how the economy works, that its opening support is thin, and that the demand-versus-dynamics credit split is unresolved. If the Committee did pursue it, I would accept only a demand-estimation citation with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. I would not broaden it to include Bresnahan or the dynamic strand, because that would change the names. My answer to the 'methods prize' objection is only partial: the method changed how market power and welfare are measured in practice. But a prize for a toolkit needs a cleaner credit structure than this one has, and that is why I no longer lead with it.

responses.point: Fredriksson answered my round-1 maturity concern directly. He argued that the finding that import exposure lowered local employment and wages is robust to the main critiques, that the dispute is about magnitudes and long-run persistence, and that prizes have regularly recognised work whose size estimates stayed contested. He also prefers a trade-shock citation to a combined technology-and-trade one because of the task-framework overlap.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. I had treated ongoing debate over magnitudes as a maturity problem. His distinction between the established discovery and the contested estimate is the right test, and B036 passes it. I keep one qualification from his own file and Teorell's: the Committee should review the shift-share exposure critiques before the citation is final, so that the wording credits the finding and the design and not a particular elasticity. I agree with his preference for the narrow trade-exposure citation over a combined one. That is why my citation names technological change only as a setting for the labour-market evidence and does not claim to credit the task framework.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, moved B036 to first place. He argued that the attribution is cleanest because the empirical programme is jointly authored by Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and that the citation should be anchored on empirical evidence about trade and labour-market adjustment and not on a general theory of technology. He placed B010 below B036 partly because its credit structure is unstable.
responses.response: I agree on the anchoring and on the credit structure, and both have shaped my citation. His comment on B010 applies equally to my own B020. A prize needs a credit structure that does not force an arbitrary cut among defensible contributors, and B020 has that problem between the demand-estimation core and the dynamic-games strand. I share his caution about the task framework, and I would add that the Committee should say openly that the citation is not a verdict on the origins of that framework. In my round-1 reply I called the merging of the two literatures my main reservation about B036. I now see that a narrow citation addresses that reservation, so the merged ballot entry does not force a merged prize.

responses.point: Enflo argued that B034 is less exposed than B036 on both maturity and overlap. She said it has no comparable dispute over magnitudes and no adjacent recent prize in the same lineage. She also read the record on B036 as more mixed than 'held up', noting that exposure measures, persistence and automation remain debated.
responses.response: She is right that B034 is the cleaner of the two on age and on the absence of a live magnitude dispute, and I rank it as an alternative for that reason. I still do not move it to first place, for two reasons. I remain less comfortable than she is with the Krugman overlap, since heterogeneous-firm selection sits inside the monopolistic-competition framework recognised in 2008. The priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is also not resolved by the evidence supplied. I accept her point that the record on B036 is mixed on magnitudes and automation. I weigh it differently now, because the debate is about size and not about whether concentrated, persistent local costs exist. I would not oppose B034 on scientific grounds, and I note that it lies close to my own work on international pricing.

responses.point: Boppart argued that later work on persistence, shift-share identification and automation has refined the magnitudes rather than reversed the sign of the effect. He also said his citation deliberately limits itself to the part of the entry where attribution is clean, and he named reconsideration conditions if the task framework could be credited without the Acemoglu overlap.
responses.response: His claim that the later literature refined magnitudes and did not reverse the sign is the empirical judgment my change rests on, and I take it as the standard to check. I accept it on the evidence recorded in the round-1 files, which I have not independently verified. I would add that the role of automation is the part of that literature least settled. That is another reason to keep technological change out of the citation as a causal claim and to describe it only as part of the setting. I agree that the task framework cannot be credited from this ballot without the Acemoglu overlap. I treat leaving out Katz and the task lineage as a real attribution cost that the Committee should record openly, not conceal.

uncertainties: How far the shift-share exposure critiques and the persistence evidence would change my view if the Committee examined them closely, and whether any specific finding would show that the central result of persistent local adjustment costs does not hold.

Whether leaving out Katz and the task-framework originators (including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, who are outside the credited names) is an acceptable attribution cost, or whether the Committee should prefer a broader technology-and-labour citation that has a harder credit structure.
Whether the overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, technology and institutions prizes should reduce the room for another award in this area.

Whether B034 would be the better choice if the Committee judged the B036 evidence too contested. That rests on the Krugman overlap and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.

My change of preference came partly from colleagues' arguments in round 1. I have tried to test those arguments on their substance, and I rely on my own knowledge of the literature without independent verification of credit attributions.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson, or to the alternatives' credited names (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Helpman, Melitz), is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose co-authorship with committee colleagues John Hassler (the chair) and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026) on a topic unrelated to these candidates. I also disclose that my research in industrial organisation and international pricing is adjacent to my alternatives B020 and B034, which could bias my judgment of them in either direction. My preferred part is in labour economics, outside my field. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact only and has no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
